traveler: Giuseppe Balsamo, called Count Alessandro di Cagliostro
title: The Grand Cophta: from the Albergheria to the Pozzetto of San Leo
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Albergheria and the Name Not Yet Invented

stops.name: Palermo, birth in the Albergheria
stops.date_confidence: attested; born 2 June 1743 and baptised 8 June, which English sources report as the birth date
stops.campa: In the Albergheria, the oldest and poorest quarter of Palermo, a son is born to the cloth merchant Pietro Balsamo and Felicita Bracconieri and is carried to the font six days later as Giuseppe. The quarter runs on the Ballaro market: fish, cheap cloth, hawkers, the noise of small trade conducted at volume. The cloth business fails and Pietro dies while the boy is small. The widow raises him on the charity of relatives. No document fixes the house and no plaque will ever mark it. The name Balsamo is the one thing he will spend his life denying.
suggested_refs: The Ballaro market and the streets of the Albergheria, Palermo

stops.name: Caltagirone, the convent apothecary
stops.date_confidence: year attested (1756); month and day unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: An uncle places the boy with a religious house in the hills near Caltagirone. English sources name the Benedictines of Santissimo Salvatore, Italian sources the Fatebenefratelli, hospitallers who keep an infirmary; the accounts have never been reconciled. Either way he is set to work beside the apothecary, learning the mortar and the still, the names of herbs, what a tincture does to a fever. He reads forbidden novels aloud during scripture, putting the names of local women in place of the saints. He is expelled, or he runs. The pharmacy stays with him for forty years.
suggested_refs: The convent infirmary and dispensary at Caltagirone where he learned pharmacy

stops.name: Palermo, Beppo Maldetto
stops.date_confidence: before his fifteenth year per en.wikipedia; the exact year is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: Back in the city he is not yet fifteen and already carries a name in the streets: Beppo Maldetto, Beppo the Cursed. The charge sheet the Inquisition assembles thirty years later begins here, with drink, gambling, brawling, forged theatre tickets, theft, extortion, and a will forged for a client who wanted an inheritance the dead man had not left him. He works with a notary's hand and a showman's nerve, and both are already finished tools. Palermo knows exactly who he is. No city he enters afterwards will.
suggested_refs: The Inquisition's charge sheet in the Compendio (Rome, 1791), which opens with the Palermo years
sources: The Life of Joseph Balsamo (London, 1791), the English Compendio

stops.name: Palermo, the olive field and the goldsmith Marano
stops.date_confidence: c.1760, at age seventeen per en.wikipedia; the pool's c.1764 is unsupported and the month is defaulted
stops.campa: He tells the goldsmith Marano that a treasure lies buried outside the walls, guarded by demons who must be paid before they give it up. Marano hands over sixty ounces of gold for the ceremony and follows him at night into an olive field. What waits there is not a demon but confederates with sticks. The goldsmith goes home beaten and poorer, convinced for a while that hell itself has done it, and then convinced otherwise. The warrant follows within days. Balsamo leaves Palermo at seventeen and never sees the city again.
suggested_refs: The olive groves outside the walls of eighteenth-century Palermo, site of the evocation

stops.name: Messina, the harbor and Althotas
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the flight follows the Marano fraud, c.1760-61; the meeting rests on Cagliostro's testimony alone
stops.campa: He lands at Messina across the strait and there, by his own account and no one else's, meets Althotas: an alchemist of no nation, speaking every language, claiming descent from the priesthood of Egypt. No port book, no witness, no letter puts a second man in that room. Here too the title goes on, taken from a dead kinswoman of his mother's line, the accounts differing on whether she was aunt or great-aunt: Count Alessandro di Cagliostro. He boards a ship as a Sicilian forger and steps off it a nobleman with a master.
stops.quote: he imagined himself to be of an illustrious family, and supposed that he was born at Naples
stops.quote_source: The Life of Joseph Balsamo, commonly called Count Cagliostro (London, 1791), p. 65, the Vatican account of his origin stories
suggested_refs: The harbor quarter of Messina before the 1783 earthquake

stops.name: Valletta, the claimed initiation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: self-reported in his memorial, undated there; the year follows the traditional account
stops.campa: In the memorial he writes later for judges, the road runs through Malta: Althotas presents him to the Grand Master Pinto, he works in the laboratory of the Knights, he is received into the order. The Knights of Malta keep excellent registers and no register carries his name. Everything about the claim is well chosen, which is the argument against it. A Sicilian without papers needs an order of chivalry to walk into a European drawing room, and Malta is the nearest one to Sicily.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Order of St John under Grand Master Pinto, which do not carry his name

stops.name: Alexandria, the harbor and the claimed priests
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: self-reported only, no independent record; month and day unknown
stops.campa: He says he sails with Althotas to Egypt and is taught in Alexandria by keepers of a wisdom older than the Church. The claim cannot be tested and it carries everything: the whole Egyptian Rite rests on it, every lodge he charters, every degree he sells, every fee. A century later this same harbor holds a lodge called Les Pyramides d'Egypte, and in 1864 it initiates Emir Abdelkader, an Egyptian lodge in Egypt receiving a man who never needed to invent a pedigree for himself.
stops.quote: he found himself in the city of Medina, was called Acharat, and lived in the house of the Mufti Salaahym
stops.quote_source: The Life of Joseph Balsamo, commonly called Count Cagliostro (London, 1791), p. 65, the Vatican account of his eastern origin narrative
suggested_refs: The Alexandria lodge Les Pyramides d'Egypte, which initiated Emir Abdelkader in 1864

stops.name: Giza, the pyramids and the chamber
stops.date_confidence: tradition, self-reported; no contemporary corroboration and no fixed date
stops.campa: Tradition, meaning his own telling, brings him to the pyramids and down into a chamber where instruction is given that may not afterwards be written. The pyramids in 1766 stand half-buried in sand and are visited by almost no Europeans, which is exactly what makes them useful: nobody in Warsaw or Strasbourg can contradict a word of it. Thirty-two years after this claimed descent a French army arrives here with surveyors and draughtsmen and begins measuring the thing to the centimetre. The imaginary Egypt is on borrowed time.
suggested_refs: The Giza plateau before the French expedition of 1798 and the Description de l'Egypte

segments.name: Rome, and the Roads of the Fugitive

stops.name: Rome, San Salvatore in Campo: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested, 21 April 1768; the church is San Salvatore in Campo in the rione Regola, not Piazza di Spagna
stops.campa: In a small church in the rione Regola, a short walk from Campo de' Fiori, he marries Lorenza Serafina Feliciani: seventeen years old, daughter of a coppersmith, unable to read. English accounts make her fourteen through an error of arithmetic; the record of her birth gives April 1751. She will travel with him for twenty-one years under half a dozen names, play the seeress at his ceremonies, be shown to princes as living proof of his elixirs, and end by denouncing him to a priest a few streets from this altar.
suggested_refs: The church of San Salvatore in Campo, rione Regola, and its marriage register

stops.name: Rome, the Marquis Agliata and the forged seals
stops.date_confidence: 1768 attested; the month is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: The newlyweds fall in with a confidence man calling himself the Marquis Agliata, and the household trade becomes papal seals, patents, and lottery tickets, all forged. Cagliostro is good at it; a seal is only a design, and he has an engraver's patience for design. The scheme is discovered, Agliata goes off with the money, and the couple leave Rome ahead of the sbirri. From here until London they are fugitives with a repertoire: relics, cures, and letters of introduction written by themselves.
suggested_refs: The Compendio's reconstruction of the Agliata forgeries, drawn from the Inquisition dossier

stops.name: Aix-en-Provence, Casanova at the same inn
stops.date_confidence: 1770 attested by Trowbridge quoting Casanova; the month is not given, and the Spanish and Portuguese years around it are dated only as a block, 1769-1772
stops.campa: Travelling as pilgrims to Compostela, with begging letters and a wooden crucifix, the Balsamos put up at an inn in Aix and find Giacomo Casanova under the same roof. He watches them and writes it down: a young woman worn out by the road, beautiful, touched with melancholy, and a husband who draws well and lies fluently. Two professionals of the same century recognize each other across a table. Barcelona, Madrid, and Lisbon follow, three years of small frauds, and Casanova is the only witness of the decade with nothing to gain by destroying them.
stops.quote: I found the female pilgrim seated in a chair looking like a person exhausted with fatigue, and interesting by reason of her youth and beauty, singularly heightened by a touch of melancholy
stops.quote_source: Casanova, Memoires, quoted in W. R. H. Trowbridge, Cagliostro (1910)
suggested_refs: Casanova's account of the Balsamos on the pilgrim road, in his Memoires

segments.name: The Mason and the Northern Courts

stops.name: London, Gerrard Street: initiation at the Esperance Lodge
stops.date_confidence: attested, 12 April 1777, by both wikipedias and the lodge minutes cited in Trowbridge
stops.campa: Returned to London in July 1776, he is initiated on the twelfth of April at the Esperance Lodge No. 289, which meets at the King's Head tavern in Gerrard Street, Soho. It is a modest lodge, largely of foreign tradesmen, in a back room over a public house. He takes the apprentice degree there and walks out holding the one thing he has never been able to forge convincingly: a real membership, conferred by an institution with branches in every capital in Europe and a habit of trusting travellers who know the signs.
suggested_refs: The minutes of Esperance Lodge No. 289, King's Head tavern, Gerrard Street, Soho

stops.name: Southwark, the King's Bench Prison
stops.date_confidence: 1777 attested; the month is not fixed in the consulted sources and is placed here
stops.campa: The London year ends badly. Creditors and an accusation of fraud put him behind the wall of the King's Bench in Southwark, the debtors' prison where a man buys better rooms if he has money and rots if he has none. He has been living as a healer and an adviser on lottery numbers, telling one client to take her children to the country and never come back through his door. He gets out stripped of what he had, and concludes that a rite with a ritual and a treasury travels better than a lottery system.
stops.quote: If you will take my advice, you will go into the country with your three children and live on the interest of your money. If I have obliged you, the only return I desire is that you will never more re-enter my doors.
stops.quote_source: Cagliostro to a Miss Fry, London, 1777, reported in W. R. H. Trowbridge, Cagliostro (1910)
suggested_refs: The King's Bench Prison, Southwark, and its rules for paying prisoners

stops.name: Mitau, the lodge among the Baltic nobility
stops.date_confidence: 1779 attested, fixed by Elisa von der Recke's later expose; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: In the capital of the Duchy of Courland he founds a lodge of his Egyptian Rite among the Baltic German nobility and finds his first true following. The von Medem family take him into their houses. He promises initiates communion with elemental spirits, transmutation of metals, and a regeneration of body and soul, and uses a child as the seer, gazing into a carafe of water while the company waits in silence. Elisa von der Recke sits in that room, believes for a season, and afterwards writes the exposure that trails him for the rest of his life.
stops.quote_source: Reported self-description, in Henry Ridgely Evans, Cagliostro and His Egyptian Rite of Freemasonry (1919), Part I
suggested_refs: Elisa von der Recke's published account of the Mitau seances
sources: Iain McCalman, The Last Alchemist (2003), at second hand
Evans, Cagliostro and His Egyptian Rite (1919)

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the Count Phoenix and the court physicians
stops.date_confidence: 1779-1780, a stay of about nine months, per ru.wikipedia; en.wikipedia's Spring 1778 would put Petersburg before Mitau and reverse the documented route, and is rejected
stops.campa: He arrives in the Russian capital under the name Count Phoenix and stays about nine months, treating the poor for nothing and the rich for a great deal, and claiming cures the college of physicians will not allow to stand. The court is amused, then irritated. Catherine, who writes comedies against mystics and lodge-masters herself, has no use for him whatever. He leaves under pressure and turns west. A Russian legend is already forming behind him, and it keeps the name Phoenix.
suggested_refs: Catherine II's anti-Masonic comedies, written in the years around his Petersburg stay

stops.name: Warsaw, the alchemy exposed
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival May 1780, departure 26 June 1780, per it.wikipedia
stops.campa: Prince Adam Poninski lodges him and gives him a laboratory, and Warsaw watches a transmutation performed before witnesses. One of the witnesses is a skeptic who keeps notes, and the notes are printed. Within six weeks the demonstration is public property as a fraud, and on the twenty-sixth of June he goes in haste. It is the first of the printed exposures to catch him while he is still in the city it concerns. He turns toward France, where a cardinal is waiting for him without yet knowing his name.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw pamphlet describing the alchemical demonstrations at Prince Poninski's house

stops.name: Strasbourg, the Palais Rohan
stops.date_confidence: arrival 19 September 1780, the Strasbourg period running to 1783 per it.wikipedia; the pool's 1781 matches neither source
stops.campa: He enters Strasbourg in September and stays three years, the best of his life. He keeps his own house, treats the poor without a fee, and works cures the city talks about for a decade. Louis de Rohan, cardinal and prince-bishop, whose palace stands on the Ill beside the cathedral, becomes first his patron and then his believer, and gives him rooms at Saverne. A churchman who wants above all to be Marie Antoinette's friend has attached himself to a man who wants above all to be believed. Both get their wish.
stops.quote: Enough ill has been said of Cagliostro. I intend to speak well of him, because I think this is always preferable providing one can.
stops.quote_source: Baron de Gleichen, quoted in W. R. H. Trowbridge, Cagliostro (1910)
suggested_refs: The Palais Rohan at Strasbourg, seat of Cardinal Louis de Rohan; the cardinal's country house at Saverne

stops.name: Bordeaux, the winter vision
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival 8 November 1783; the vision is placed between February and May 1784
stops.campa: He arrives in Bordeaux on the eighth of November and stays the winter, practising medicine and gathering a following of merchants and gentry. Ill during those months, he reports a vision, and out of it comes the decision that ends in San Leo: to constitute the Egyptian Rite formally, with degrees, a mother lodge, a liturgy, and himself as Grand Cophta at the head of it. What has been a story about Egypt becomes an institution with officers, initiation fees, and correspondence.
suggested_refs: The Bordeaux months of 1783-1784, when the Egyptian Rite took institutional form

stops.name: Lyon, La Sagesse Triomphante
stops.date_confidence: attested, 20 October 1784; the alias Comte Phoenix belongs to Russia in 1779-80, not to Lyon
stops.campa: On the twentieth of October he founds the mother lodge of the Egyptian Rite at Lyon and calls it La Sagesse Triomphante. Men and women are admitted in linked ceremonies. The rite promises physical and moral regeneration: forty days of retreat, diet, and prayer, at the end of which the initiate is made new in body and soul. Daughter lodges are chartered from here across France. He signs as Comte de Cagliostro, the name under which he will be tried, and takes an oath of blind obedience from every man who kneels.
stops.quote: I promise, I engage, and I swear, that I will never reveal the secrets which shall be communicated to me in this temple, and that I will blindly obey my superiors.
stops.quote_source: Apprentice-degree oath of the Egyptian Rite, in Henry Ridgely Evans, Cagliostro and His Egyptian Rite of Freemasonry (1919), Part IV
suggested_refs: The mother lodge La Sagesse Triomphante at Lyon and its charters to daughter lodges
sources: Evans, Cagliostro and His Egyptian Rite (1919)

stops.name: Venice, a patent claimed for the Rite of Misraim
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Misraim origin is disputed and wholly undated; the year follows the rite's own claim and is placed after Lyon, and the place follows en.wikipedia, which puts the origin in Venice and Naples only on the onward route
stops.campa: The Rite of Misraim is said to begin in the Republic of Venice with a patent issued by Cagliostro, and to travel from there through the Franco-Italian lodges of the Kingdom of Naples until the Bedarride brothers carry it into Paris in 1814. He has been dead nineteen years by then. The document that would prove the patent has never been produced, then or since. A signature nobody has seen does steady work in the world for two hundred years, in cities he never reached.
suggested_refs: The claimed Cagliostro patent behind the Rite of Misraim, never produced

segments.name: Paris: The Necklace and the Bastille

stops.name: Paris, the house on the Rue Saint-Claude
stops.date_confidence: attested: he reaches Paris 30 January 1785, lodging first at the Palais Royal and then in the Marais
stops.campa: He takes a grand house in the Marais and Paris comes to it: seances by candlelight, a child seer at a carafe of water, Egyptian ceremonies for duchesses, two lodges founded inside the year. The city is at the top of its appetite for invisible forces. Franz Anton Mesmer has been magnetizing patients around a tub of iron filings since 1778, and Etteilla is selling an Egyptian pedigree for the tarot from a shop across the river. Cagliostro arrives late into a crowded market and is at once the most famous man in it.
stops.quote_source: Cagliostro's self-description, quoted in Henry Ridgely Evans, Cagliostro and His Egyptian Rite of Freemasonry (1919), Part I
suggested_refs: The house on the Rue Saint-Claude in the Marais, seat of his Paris ceremonies

stops.name: Versailles, the cardinal arrested in the Hall of Mirrors
stops.date_confidence: attested: Rohan is arrested 15 August 1785, Jeanne de Valois-Saint-Remy three days later, Cagliostro about a week after Rohan
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption, vested to say mass before the court, Cardinal de Rohan is taken in the Hall of Mirrors by order of the king. He has bought a diamond necklace of one million six hundred thousand livres for a queen who never wanted it, on letters forged by Jeanne de Valois-Saint-Remy and on a night meeting in a garden with a woman hired to play Marie Antoinette. The necklace is already broken up and sold in London. Louis XVI, who a year ago set a royal commission on Mesmer, now has a scandal that outlives his throne.
suggested_refs: The Galerie des Glaces at Versailles, where Rohan was arrested in his vestments

stops.name: Paris, the Bastille: seized on the Rue Saint-Claude
stops.date_confidence: attested: he is taken around 22-23 August 1785, a week after Rohan and in a different place
stops.campa: A week after the cardinal, the police come to the Rue Saint-Claude for Cagliostro and Serafina. He is handled roughly and remembers it precisely enough to write it down afterwards for a court. Nine months in the Bastille follow while the affair swells into the most-read trial in Europe and the pamphlets multiply on both sides of the Channel. Historians since have found no evidence that he had any part in the fraud. He is in the dock because he was the cardinal's magician, which in the summer of 1785 is explanation enough.
stops.quote: Des Brunieres laid hold of me by the collar
stops.quote_source: Memorial for the Comte de Cagliostro, Plaintiff, versus Maitre Chesnon Junior and le Sieur de Launay, Defendants (1786), his own account of the arrest
suggested_refs: The Bastille cells above the ditch, where he was held nine months
sources: Memorial for the Comte de Cagliostro (1786)

stops.name: Paris, the Parlement acquits
stops.date_confidence: attested, 31 May 1786, by both wikipedias and the trial verdict
stops.campa: On the thirty-first of May the Parlement of Paris acquits the cardinal, Cagliostro, and Serafina, and condemns Jeanne de Valois-Saint-Remy to be whipped, branded with a V for voleuse, and shut in the Salpetriere. Crowds wait outside the Palais de Justice and carry him home through the streets. It is the summit of his life: a Palermo forger cleared by the highest court in France and cheered by people who have read his defence as a pamphlet, in an edition his own printer could not keep up with.
stops.quote: he denied every thing to his judges with the utmost intrepidity
stops.quote_source: The Life of Joseph Balsamo (London, 1791), p. 64, the Vatican biography describing his defiance before the Paris judges in the necklace affair
suggested_refs: The verdict of the Parlement of Paris, 31 May 1786, in the Affair of the Diamond Necklace

stops.name: Boulogne, the crossing to Dover
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure from Boulogne for Dover, 19 June 1786
stops.campa: Acquitted by the court and expelled by the king, he is given twenty-four hours to leave Paris and three weeks to leave the kingdom. On the nineteenth of June a crowd sees him off at Boulogne and he sails for Dover. He is famous in every capital in Europe and has nowhere to live in any of them. The order removing him is signed by the same hand that will be tried by a revolutionary convention and cut off in a public square seven years later, three streets from the prison he has just left.
stops.quote: An order for me to quit Paris in twenty-four hours, and the kingdom within three weeks
stops.quote_source: Memorial for the Comte de Cagliostro, Plaintiff, versus Maitre Chesnon Junior and le Sieur de Launay, Defendants (1786)
suggested_refs: The lettre de cachet expelling Cagliostro from France, June 1786
sources: Memorial for the Comte de Cagliostro (1786)

stops.name: London, the Lettre au peuple francais
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Lettre au peuple francais is dated London, 20 June 1786; it is a separate document from the 1787 letter to the English people
stops.campa: The day after he lands he dates an open letter to the French people, printed and reprinted across the Channel. In it he sets down what he saw of French justice from inside a fortress, and writes that he will come back when the Bastille has been pulled down and its ground turned into a public walk. Three years and a month later the prison falls and the walk is made. Every account of the day quotes him. A man who spent his life manufacturing prophecies is remembered for the one that arrived on time.
suggested_refs: The Lettre au peuple francais, London, 20 June 1786, with its passage on the Bastille
sources: Memorial for the Comte de Cagliostro (1786)

stops.name: London, Morande and the letter to the English people
stops.date_confidence: 1787 per en.wikipedia; the month is not fixed, and this letter is distinct from the Lettre au peuple francais of June 1786
stops.campa: Charles Theveneau de Morande, blackmailer turned journalist, prints in the Courier de l'Europe the reconstruction that undoes him: the count is Giuseppe Balsamo of Palermo, forger, and here are the dates and the witnesses. Cagliostro answers with an open letter to the English people denying it, and forces a retraction out of the paper. The retraction changes nothing at all. From here the biography is public property, and every city he enters has read the Sicilian version before he reaches the gate.
suggested_refs: Theveneau de Morande's exposures in the Courier de l'Europe, 1786-1787

stops.name: Palermo, Goethe at the Balsamo house
stops.date_confidence: April 1787 per Goethe's Italienische Reise; the exact day is not fixed and is placed here
stops.campa: Goethe, travelling in Sicily, decides to test the story at its source. With an introduction and a false errand he finds the family of Giuseppe Balsamo living in poverty in Palermo, a mother and a sister who speak of a relative gone abroad and long unheard from. He gives them money and goes, and writes afterwards that he wishes he had done more. The count is shown to be a Palermo widow's son by a poet with a notebook, four years before the Holy Office proves the same thing with a dossier.
suggested_refs: Goethe's Italienische Reise, the Palermo chapters of April 1787

stops.name: Turin, refused by the King of Sardinia
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure toward Aix-les-Bains and Turin dated 23 July 1788 by it.wikipedia; the expulsions from Switzerland and Savoy precede it
stops.campa: Switzerland, Savoy, and then Turin close to him one after another; the King of Sardinia will not have him in his states. He pawns what is left, travels with fewer servants each season, and finds that lodges which once paid for degrees no longer answer his letters. The Egyptian Rite owns no property, holds no charter from any authority but himself, and has no protector left anywhere. He moves toward Italy because there is nowhere else to go, and Italy is where the Holy Office keeps its files.
suggested_refs: The successive expulsions from Switzerland, Savoy, and the states of the King of Sardinia, 1787-1788

stops.name: Trento, the bishop writes to Rome
stops.date_confidence: 25 March 1789 per it.wikipedia; the letter itself is known only at second hand, so the entry stands as reconstruction
stops.campa: At Trento, sheltered by the prince-bishop, he goes to mass, speaks of returning to the Church, and is told that Rome might be persuaded to receive him. On the twenty-fifth of March the bishop writes to the Curia in his favour and calls him repentant. It is the last time an institution takes his side in writing. Serafina, worn out and homesick, presses for Rome. He knows what Rome does to Freemasons, and on the seventeenth of May he takes the road south with her.
suggested_refs: The bishop of Trento's letter of 25 March 1789 to the Roman Curia

stops.name: Rome, the return and the denunciation
stops.date_confidence: departure from Trento 17 May 1789 with arrival about ten days later; the lodging is placed in the rione Regola because the denunciation goes to the parish priest of Santa Caterina della Rota, against a rival account putting them at Piazza di Spagna
stops.campa: They leave Trento on the seventeenth of May and reach Rome about ten days later, taking lodgings in the crowded rioni by the river. He is warned that a Mason has no business in the papal capital, receives visitors anyway, and talks of founding a lodge in the city of the Holy Office. In September Serafina goes to the parish priest of Santa Caterina della Rota and denounces her husband: he mistreats her, he keeps her from her religion, he practises what the Church has condemned. She has been with him twenty-one years.
suggested_refs: The parish of Santa Caterina della Rota in the rione Regola, where the denunciation was made

stops.name: Castel Sant'Angelo, taken by the Inquisition
stops.date_confidence: 27 December 1789 per it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia gives 29 December and the disagreement is unresolved
stops.campa: The Holy Office arrests him with Serafina and a Capuchin friar for attempting to establish a lodge in Rome, and shuts him inside Hadrian's tomb on the Tiber. Freemasonry is a capital offence under papal law. For fifteen months he is interrogated, and he talks: about Althotas, about Medina, about a childhood he cannot place, about parents he says he never knew and a country he cannot name. The tribunal writes all of it down, and the record it makes outlives every version of himself he ever sold to anyone.
stops.quote: He confessed that he was unacquainted either with his parents or his country.
stops.quote_source: The Life of Joseph Balsamo, commonly called Count Cagliostro (London, 1791), pp. 65-66, the Vatican account of his examination
suggested_refs: Castel Sant'Angelo, papal fortress and prison of the Holy Office

stops.name: Rome, the Holy Office pronounces death
stops.date_confidence: attested, 21 March 1791, per it.wikipedia; the commutation follows on 7 April and the public proclamation on 13 April
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of March the Congregation of the Holy Office finds him guilty of heresy, magic, and Freemasonry, and fixes the penalty at death by burning. It is the same tribunal, working from the same prison beside the Vatican, that held Giordano Bruno for seven years before the fire and that held Tommaso Campanella through his interrogations. Two centuries lie between the philosopher of the infinite worlds and the seller of Egyptian degrees. The institution does not distinguish between them.
suggested_refs: The prison of the Holy Office beside the Vatican, which held Bruno, Campanella, and Cagliostro

stops.name: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, the abjuration and the burning
stops.date_confidence: attested: the sentence is proclaimed and abjured 13 April 1791, the commutation by Pius VI having been signed on 7 April; the site is the Minerva, not Campo de' Fiori
stops.campa: On the seventh of April Pius VI commutes the fire to perpetual imprisonment. On the thirteenth the sentence is read in public and he abjures on his knees in the Dominican church raised over the ruins of Minerva's temple, while his manuscripts, his instruments, and the ritual of the Egyptian Rite burn in the square. The same decree condemns Egyptian Masonry itself as heresy. No authenticated original of the ritual survives anywhere; every lodge that has claimed the rite since works from descriptions of what was burned here.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, site of the public abjuration and the burning of the Egyptian Rite papers

stops.name: San Leo, the transfer to the Rocca
stops.date_confidence: attested, 20 April 1791; the fortress stands in the Montefeltro, province of Rimini, not in the Tuscan-Romagnol Apennines
stops.campa: A week after the abjuration he is taken north into the Montefeltro and up the single road that climbs the rock of San Leo, where a fortress rebuilt for Federico da Montefeltro by the Sienese engineer Francesco di Giorgio Martini stands on a cliff over the valley. There is no wall here worth scaling and no gate worth bribing; the mountain is the prison and the garrison is a formality. He is put in the Stanza del Tesoro, the treasury room, which has a window. For five months he can still see the horizon.
suggested_refs: The Forte di San Leo, rebuilt by Francesco di Giorgio Martini for Federico da Montefeltro

stops.name: San Leo, the Pozzetto
stops.date_confidence: attested, 11 September 1791, per it.wikipedia
stops.campa: On the eleventh of September he is moved to the cell they call il Pozzetto, the little well: three metres by three, no door of any kind, entered through a trapdoor in the ceiling by which food is lowered to him. The window is cut down to a slit behind triple bars, set so that he can see the two churches of the town and nothing else of the world. Popular tradition says he was walled up alive here. The chaplain's record says he was not. The two accounts agree entirely on what the room was for.
suggested_refs: The cell called il Pozzetto in the Rocca di San Leo, entered by a ceiling trapdoor

stops.name: San Leo, the letters to the Pope
stops.date_confidence: December 1793 per it.wikipedia; the letters are known only through the fortress record, so the entry stands as reconstruction
stops.campa: After two years in the hole he obtains permission to write to Pius VI, and writes about visions: figures that come to him in the dark, instructions, a message he says is meant for the Pope alone and for no secretary. The letters go down the mountain and are read by officials who file them as the ravings of a prisoner or the last manoeuvre of a confidence man. No answer comes back up. The Grand Cophta of the Egyptian Rite is by now a man in a stone box asking a Pope to believe him.
suggested_refs: The San Leo fortress register of his petitions and letters, 1793

stops.name: Rome, Serafina dies at Sant'Apollonia
stops.date_confidence: 1794 attested, at the age of forty-three; the month is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: Serafina, who denounced him and was shut up in a convent for her pains, dies at Sant'Apollonia in Trastevere at forty-three. She was married at seventeen and spent the years between in his ceremonies, playing the seeress, the countess, the pilgrim, the patient restored by his elixir, whatever the room required that season. The Holy Office treated her first as a witness and then as a penitent. The house that held her buries her, and her grave, like her husband's, is not marked.
suggested_refs: The convent of Sant'Apollonia in Trastevere, where Lorenza Serafina Feliciani died

stops.name: San Leo, the death in the Pozzetto
stops.date_confidence: attested: found semi-paralysed 23 August 1795, dead about 22:30 on 26 August, aged fifty-two
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of August he is found half-paralysed on the floor of the cell after a stroke. He lies three days in an apoplectic state, refusing the confession and the penitence the chaplain presses on him, and dies about half past ten on the night of the twenty-sixth, fifty-two years old. Fra Cristoforo da Cicerchia writes in the register that the justice of God has been done on an impious man. They bury him on the hill without a coffin and without a stone, like an infidel unworthy of the suffrages of the Holy Church.
suggested_refs: The chaplain's register of San Leo, kept by fra Cristoforo da Cicerchia
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Alessandro Cagliostro', citing the chaplain's account

segments.name: The Prosecution's Book and the Afterlife

stops.name: Rome, the Compendio printed at the Vatican press
stops.date_confidence: published in Rome in 1791, after the April sentence; the month is not fixed and is placed here
stops.campa: The Apostolic press publishes the Compendio della vita e delle gesta di Giuseppe Balsamo, the tribunal's own account of its own trial, and translations follow into French, English, and German inside the year. It is written to destroy him and it becomes, for a century, the principal source for his life. Every biographer of the next hundred years works from the depositions of a prosecution, and several of them notice that the book fed the reputation it was built to end. He is left in the keeping of his enemies' prose.
suggested_refs: Compendio della vita e delle gesta di Giuseppe Balsamo (Rome, Typographia Apostolica Vaticana, 1791) and its translations
sources: The Life of Joseph Balsamo (London, 1791), the English Compendio

stops.name: Weimar, Der Gross-Cophta on stage
stops.date_confidence: attested: premiere at the Weimar court theatre, 17 December 1791
stops.campa: Four years after finding the Balsamo family in Palermo, Goethe puts the necklace affair on the stage of the Weimar court theatre as a comedy, with the Grand Cophta as a lodge-master fleecing the credulous. It fails with the audience. He goes on returning to the affair for years, reading it as the first visible crack in the French monarchy: a queen's name for sale, a cardinal deceived by forged letters, and a Sicilian in the middle of it whom the highest court in France could not convict.
suggested_refs: Goethe, Der Gross-Cophta (1791), and its premiere at the Weimar court theatre
sources: Goethe, Der Gross-Cophta (1791) and its stage history

stops.name: San Leo, the Polish troops and the skull
stops.date_confidence: December 1797 attested for the occupation and the disturbance of the remains; everything concerning the skull is local tradition only and no relic has been produced
stops.campa: Two years after his death, Polish troops in French service take the fortress and free the prisoners, and in the disorder the graves on the hill are opened. What became of the remains is story from that point on. San Leo has told for generations that the skull was kept and drunk from, and one version makes it a cup for Napoleon himself. No contemporary record supports any of it. Napoleon's army will be in Egypt within a year, measuring the pyramids Cagliostro claimed to have entered.
stops.quote: a few years after the Count's death, Polish troops, allied with the French, arrived and occupied the fort giving freedom to the convicts who, with the help of soldiers, dug up the Count's pits and used his skull as a cup in which to consume alcohol
stops.quote_source: Local San Leo tradition as repeated in regional histories of the fortress
suggested_refs: The 1797 occupation of the Rocca di San Leo and the local tradition of the skull

stops.name: Paris, Dumas makes him the engine of the Revolution
stops.date_confidence: serialization runs 1846-1848; the month is not fixed and is defaulted
stops.campa: Alexandre Dumas begins serializing Joseph Balsamo and opens his Marie Antoinette cycle with Cagliostro at the centre of it, not a swindler but an immortal adept steering France toward 1789 on purpose. The novel reaches more readers in ten years than the Compendio reached in fifty, and it is the version that survives. The forger who could not get the world to believe him while he lived is believed thoroughly afterwards, in a shape he did not write, by readers born after his death.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Dumas, Joseph Balsamo, or Memoires d'un medecin, serialized 1846-1848
sources: Publication history of Dumas, Joseph Balsamo

stops.name: Manchester, the Egyptian Rite line handed on
stops.date_confidence: 24 September 1902 per theodor_reuss.journey.json; the descent from Cagliostro's own rite is claimed by the tradition and is not documented
stops.campa: John Yarker confers the Rite of Memphis and Misraim on Theodor Reuss, continuing a chain of succession claimed back to Cagliostro's own Egyptian Rite. The chain is asserted backward through the nineteenth century to a patent nobody has produced, and from there to a Sicilian who said he had been taught in a chamber under the pyramids. The unbroken pedigree he could never secure in life is supplied to him a century afterwards, by men who never met him and never doubted him.
suggested_refs: John Yarker's 1902 charter of the Rite of Memphis and Misraim to Theodor Reuss

stops.name: San Leo, the cell shown to visitors
stops.date_confidence: present state; the fortress operates as a museum under the Musei Nazionali dell'Emilia-Romagna
stops.campa: The Rocca is a state museum now, with a weapons collection and a picture gallery, and the thing visitors climb the road for is the Pozzetto. There is no tomb and no monument; the grave dug on this hill in 1795 was never marked, and the bones were scattered two years later. What survives of him is a room three metres square, the printed case his prosecutors made against him, and a rite that living lodges still work from reconstructions of a text burned at the Minerva.
suggested_refs: The Forte di San Leo museum and the preserved cell of the Pozzetto
